generatedProse.concept-context: Across disciplines, a reference list is read closely. It shows whether you have engaged with the key work, the recent work, and the dissenting voices, so it signals the scope of your reading. How you use those sources shows your critical edge: whether you simply cite an influential finding or set it against one that challenges it. A reader going through your citations is reading how you think about evidence, not only checking that you have not copied.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Two students submit essays that both avoid plagiarism and both reference correctly.

Student A cites a source after almost every sentence, each one a respected name, each dropped in to back a point already made. The citations are accurate and the list is long. But they all pull the same way: no source is set against another, so the reader sees reading, not thinking. The references prove Student A did the reading, and little more.

Student B cites fewer sources but uses them against one another: one source is introduced, then qualified by a later one that challenges it, and the paragraph reaches a position of its own. The same conventions now carry a visibly critical argument. The reader can see Student B weighing the evidence, not just reporting it.

Both reference correctly. Only Student B made the references work as evidence of thinking, which is what they are for.
generatedProse.summary: Referencing does far more than keep you clear of plagiarism. It credits the authors you build on and lets others credit you, so a field's conversation can accumulate over time. It also signals the scope of your reading and the critical edge of your thinking, such as weighing one source against another that challenges it. You can now justify referencing as joining a conversation, explain what references tell a reader, and defend referencing on grounds stronger than fear of a penalty. The last lesson turns to the judgement involved in using sources well.

check.body: In the worked example, why did Student B's references show a stronger critical edge than Student A's?

items.text: Student B set sources against one another, such as one finding against another that challenges it, to reach a position.
Student B cited far more sources than Student A did.
Student B placed a citation after almost every sentence.
Student B chose more respected names than Student A did.

feedback.correct: That's right. Setting sources against one another, rather than stacking agreement, is the critical edge a reader can see.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Think about what Student B did with the sources, not how many there were.
feedback.incorrectFinal: The critical edge came from setting sources against one another to reach a position. Citing more, citing after every sentence, or citing well-known names does not show thinking by itself.

_prompts.concept-context: What does this look like in practice within the given context? Write a short follow-on from the generic definition above, in the learner's own subject or discipline. Keep it to two or three sentences, mid-register, following straight on from the generic definition.
_prompts.worked-example: Give a subject-specific worked example of this lesson's concept: a weaker or less-developed version first, then a stronger version reached by better practice, using the context cast (character tokens) consistently. Keep the weaker-then-stronger shape and the two-part contrast; carry the cast only through the {{learner-a}} (weaker) and {{learner-b}} (stronger) tokens, never a literal name (the pack supplies the whole body, but not the names). Each example paragraph must begin with its token, weaker first - merge-context.js's wrapProse() only emits the we-weaker/we-stronger cue classes for a paragraph that leads with the token. The merge renders it as a block quote, so write it as continuous prose, not as a quoted comment plus commentary.
_prompts.summary: Recap what the learner can now do, in terms of their own subject or context. One short paragraph. Do not restate the learning outcomes verbatim.
_prompts.check: Write the subject's own version of this lesson's check question(s), testing the same outcome in the learner's own discipline. Keep the same number of items and the same correctness pattern as the generic version; reword the stem and items for the subject. Keep the component-level feedback (correct / notFinal / final) teaching, never a bare verdict.
